k006: Curious about people, cultures and business.
k012: Everywhere I go, people want the same things. To belong. To be safe. To be taken seriously. To love and be loved. What changes is how each culture says it.
k013: I've seen where that ends. In Iraq I interviewed Syrian refugees. In Rwanda, survivors of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. Hate rarely starts with violence. It starts when we stop seeing each other as human.

k023: * Source: Ethnologue 2026 via Wikipedia. Total speakers, native and second language: English 1,530M, Spanish 561M, Arabic 411M, French 334M, Portuguese 269M, Indonesian 255M, Swedish 13M, Danish 6M. Together about 3.4 billion; counting people who speak more than one of them only once gives close to 3 billion (estimate). Native speakers: Spanish 487M, English 450M, Arabic 411M, Portuguese 252M, Indonesian 78M, French 75M, Swedish 10M, Danish 5.5M. Official language reach: more than 4.5 billion people live in a country where one of them is official (World Bank population data, 2018). Map: coral shows countries where most people grow up speaking one of them. Green: countries where one of them is an official language, used in business, government and school, but not most people's mother tongue.
k025: Understanding people on their terms, not mine.
k026: A language carries far more than words. It holds a culture's humour, its history, its codes of politeness, its biases and the things it never needs to say out loud.
k027: When I speak with someone in their mother tongue, I'm running on their operating system instead of my own. I hear the joke the way it was meant. I notice the assumptions built into the language, and the ones built into mine.
k028: That's where real connection starts. Learning a language is learning a way of seeing the world. Perspective is everything.
k031: At school in Herlev I was the troublemaker, and a counsellor told me to forget about law. In 2017, at 26, I became Denmark's youngest lawyer.
k032: From troubled kid to Denmark's youngest lawyer
k038: "I'm not in it for the attention"
k044: Former board member of Amnesty International Denmark. Dignity first, and every side heard.
k046: Since 2014 I've helped startups and scaleups build and run their operations across the world.
k048: Board member at Chapters Institute. Advisor to several promising startups. Building a language app of my own.
k062: AI will change the world. Everyone should understand it.
k063: I've spent years nerding out on AI: how it works, what it can do, and how it can be used for us and against us.
k064: The world is on the cusp of massive, irreversible change. Some of it for good, some of it for bad. Right now, understanding AI is a privilege. I want to make it accessible to everyone, in plain words, because all of us need that literacy to have a say in what comes next.
k067: A short letter every Sunday. One idea, from where I'm standing. Free.
k068: The first letters are on Substack.
k074: Short bio for press and events
k075: Mousta M. Moustafa is a Danish lawyer, founder and former board member of Amnesty International Denmark. In 2017, at 26, he became Denmark's youngest lawyer. Since 2014 he has helped startups and scaleups build and operate across the world, closing deals in more than 50 countries. He speaks eight languages, has visited more than 100 countries, sits on the board of Chapters Institute and has given two TEDx talks.

k012b: Right now, we're losing the ability to hear it. Our feeds show us more of what we already believe, until people on the other side stop looking like people.
k013b: So I try to do the opposite: understand people on their terms, see the world from where they stand, and build bridges from there. Companies, stories and conversations that put people in the same room.
k013c: Peace, love and dignity. Not for one people. For all.
